title: Ben Graham & the Growth Investor | Hewitt Heiserman | Talks at Google
description:
Hewitt Heiserman authored "It's Earnings That Count" and is finishing his second book, “The Checklist Investor”. He is a member of the Boston Security Analyst Society and CFA Institute. He has written for several investing publications.. He graduated from Kenyon College and received the Faculty Award for Distinguished Achievement. He is an Ironman finisher, and is active in open land preservation.

The slides to pair with this talk can be found at: https://goo.gl/kg1BtL
summary: The talk argues that investors should distinguish between high-quality compounders with durable competitive advantages and cyclical or distressed assets. The speaker highlights specific technology and consumer stocks that have historically delivered explosive growth, noting that Ben Graham would have valued Google based on net working capital while acknowledging its strong earnings trajectory. Conversely, the discussion warns against buying assets that have fallen below their 200-day moving averages, citing significant losses in energy, banking, and broader market indices as evidence of bearish signals.

claims.claim: The speaker notes that Ben Graham would have bought Google for $48 per share based on a net working capital calculation.
claims.quote: You've got 745 million shares outstanding, so he'd paid $45. Is that right? $48 for Google. All right. That's what he would buy it for.
claims.speaker: HEWITT HEISERMAN

claims.claim: The speaker describes Monster Beverage as the best performing stock of the last 20 years, growing a hypothetical $10,000 into $10 million.
claims.quote: Monster's interesting because this is the best performing stock of the last 20 years. A hypothetical $10000 investment grew to $10 million.
claims.speaker: HEWITT HEISERMAN

claims.claim: Morningstar estimates Alphabet's intrinsic value at $755 a share, while the stock price was $682, representing a 90% price to intrinsic value ratio.
claims.quote: Morningstar-- they do a lot of great work with estimating companies intrinsic value. They project that the business-- Alphabet's worth $755 a share. The stock price as of last week was $682. So the price to intrinsic value is 90%.
claims.speaker: HEWITT HEISERMAN

claims.claim: Warren Buffett determined American Express' franchise was intact after a scandal and put 40% of partnership funds into it, which went up five-fold in five years.
claims.quote: Mr. Buffet determined that American Express' franchise was intact, and he put 40% of the partnerships funds into American Express and it then went up five-fold in five years.
claims.speaker: HEWITT HEISERMAN

claims.claim: Microsoft is described as a 100 bagger that turned a hypothetical $10,000 into a million dollars during the 1990s with high quality earnings and explosive growth.
claims.quote: Here is Microsoft during the 1990s. Remember, this company turned a hypothetical $10,000 into a million dollars. This is what we call-- to use Peter Lynch's description, a 100 bagger.
claims.speaker: HEWITT HEISERMAN

claims.claim: Cisco Systems turned a hypothetical $10,000 investment into $631,000, showing a positive trajectory in high quality earnings.
claims.quote: Cisco Systems, $10 grand into $631,000.
claims.speaker: HEWITT HEISERMAN

claims.claim: Paychex turned a hypothetical $10,000 investment into $257,000, demonstrating profitable growth and a competitive advantage.
claims.speaker: HEWITT HEISERMAN

claims.claim: Hansen Natural turned a hypothetical $10,000 investment into $2.6 million, showing a positive trajectory in high quality earnings.
claims.quote: Hansen Natural, $10,000 into $2.6 million.
claims.speaker: HEWITT HEISERMAN

claims.claim: Dell Computer turned a hypothetical $10,000 investment into $1.3 million, showing a positive trajectory in high quality earnings.
claims.quote: Dell Computer, $10 grand into $1.3 million.
claims.speaker: HEWITT HEISERMAN

claims.claim: The speaker notes that Alphabet made $14.4 billion in earnings by 2014, exceeding the $10 billion prediction he made in December 2004.
claims.quote: I said that it was unlikely that Google would make $14 billion dollars of earnings by 2014. Actually I said $10 billion. In fact you made $14.4 billion. So congratulations.
claims.speaker: Hewitt Heiserman

claims.claim: The speaker cites Amazon's price to earnings ratio as 114, noting that it would take 114 years to get the stock price purchase back if earnings remained constant.
claims.quote: Amazon's price is about $507. It's going to earn about $4.46 this year. So its price to earnings ratio is 114. If Amazon makes that same level of earnings forever, you'll wait 114 years to get your stock price purchase back.
claims.speaker: Hewitt Heiserman

claims.claim: The speaker states that Alphabet's price to earnings ratio is about 20 times earnings.
claims.quote: Alphabet's about 20 times earnings. The market's about 21 times earnings and then Apple about 10 times earnings.
claims.speaker: Hewitt Heiserman

claims.claim: The speaker reports that Alphabet made almost $75 billion in revenue and $16.4 billion in net income for 2015.
claims.quote: You made almost $75 billion. So I'm in the GAAP column right now. You made $75 billion of revenue. You had $59 billion of expenses. Your net income is $16.4 billion.
claims.speaker: Hewitt Heiserman

claims.claim: The speaker notes that Alphabet had earnings per share of almost $22 a share for 2015.
claims.quote: Your net income is $16.4 billion. And earnings per share almost $22 a share.
claims.speaker: Hewitt Heiserman

claims.claim: The speaker states that Alphabet made an investment of $8.5 billion in fixed capital last year.
claims.quote: So in Alphabet's case last year you made an investment of $8.5 billion dollars. So that's a $8.5 billion of cash that's coming out of your corporate checking account that does not appear in the GAAP income statement.
claims.speaker: Hewitt Heiserman

claims.claim: The speaker notes that Microsoft was a bullish trend for most of the 1990s as the stock price stayed above its 200-day moving average.
claims.quote: Here's Microsoft's stock price versus 200-day moving average during the 1990s. You can see that for most of the time-- most of the time the blue line, the moving average was like a support level. There were a couple of times when the price went below the 200-day moving average, but by and large the closing price was always above the 200-day moving average. So by and large this is a bullish trend.
claims.speaker: Hewitt Heiserman

claims.claim: The speaker indicates that Alphabet is 6% above its 200-day moving average, which is a positive sign if using the 200-day moving average approach.
claims.quote: You're probably asking, what about Alphabet? Well, you're 6% above the 200-day moving average. So this is a positive sign if you're using this approach.
claims.speaker: Hewitt Heiserman

claims.claim: The speaker sold Interactive Brokers after it went below its 200-day moving average and subsequently fell 24%.
claims.quote: Interactive Brokers is a stock that I own, but I sold after I noticed that it went below its 200-day moving average. And you can see that it then fell 24%.
claims.speaker: Hewitt Heiserman

claims.claim: The speaker describes Deutsche Bank as down 45% and a sell signal because it fell below its 200-day moving average.
claims.quote: Deutsche Bank is down 45%. It fell below its 200-day moving average. And this an important bank to watch because as Deutsche Bank goes, I think Europe will go too. They've got $70 trillion of derivatives. And if you own the bank, this would have been a sell signal.
claims.speaker: Hewitt Heiserman

claims.claim: The speaker notes that oil prices are now 70% below their 200-day moving average.
claims.quote: You're probably aware that oil prices have gone down. Oil is now 70% below its 200-day moving average. So you if you had sold in August of 2014 at about $100, congratulations. The last price is about $31.
claims.speaker: Hewitt Heiserman

claims.claim: The speaker points out that Horsehead Holding is down 99.48% in less than one year.
claims.quote: Horsehead Holding is down 99.48% in less than one year. Look how violently some of these companies can collapse.
claims.speaker: Hewitt Heiserman

claims.claim: The speaker states that Linn Energy is down 99% since it went below its 200-day moving average.
claims.quote: Linn Energy, down 99% since it went below its 200-day moving average. Now, probably some of you are math majors. So check this out. After Linn went below its 200-day moving average it fell 50% to $14.
claims.speaker: Hewitt Heiserman

claims.company: Vanguard total stock market index fund
claims.claim: The speaker notes that the Vanguard total stock market index fund is in bear territory because the current close is below the 200-day moving average.
claims.quote: This is Vanguard's total stock market index fund. The 200-day moving average is $50.60. And then Friday's close was $45.92. So this means we're in bear territory.
claims.speaker: Hewitt Heiserman

claims.claim: The speaker interprets that Paul Tudor Jones would be bullish on corporate bonds because the index is above its 200-day moving average.
claims.quote: This is a Vanguard index fund. And then the average of the last 200 days of closing prices is $22.50-- $22.60. So on this basis, Paul Tudor Jones-- I don't want to put words in his mouth, but my interpretation is he would be bullish on corporate bonds.
claims.speaker: Hewitt Heiserman
